chapters.title: Chapter 1: In the Presence of Danger

assets.topic: The Voice Kelly Disliked (Intuition vs. Politeness)
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen shows a dimly lit stairwell in an older apartment building. Kelly, a twenty-seven-year-old counselor, stands on the third-floor landing clutching torn grocery bags while cans of cat food roll down the stairs. A friendly-looking young man bounds up the steps collecting cans, smiles, and offers to carry her bags. An on-screen live cue feed lets the player scrub through the encounter second by second.
assets.player_mission: Scrub through the interaction and mark the exact moments where the man's behavior transmits a warning. Then choose the cue that was present before Kelly had any conscious reason for alarm.
key_concepts: Kelly disliked the stranger's voice right from the start, and the feeling arrived before she had any concrete reason; de Becker treats that early unease as real information.
The man's offer to carry her groceries was unsolicited; he volunteered help she never asked for and then refused to accept her decline.
Kelly's intuition registered pre-incident indicators, detectable factors occurring before the outcome, below her conscious awareness.
She felt guilty about her suspicion of a friendly, gentlemanly man, and guilt, politeness, and the wish not to distrust everybody are the social forces that suppress survival signals.
When Kelly finally handed over the grocery bag, she signaled to him, and to herself, that she was willing to trust him: as the bag passed from her control to his, so did she.
The man used rapport and charm, the friendly smile and the shared hungry-cat joke, while engineering proximity to her apartment door.
His persistence escalated in graded steps: refusing her no, tugging at her bag, then proposing to enter with the door left open like ladies do in old movies.
de Becker's core claim is that every person has a brilliant internal guardian that stands ready to warn of hazards and guide them through risky situations.
Victims who later say it came out of nowhere will, when asked quietly, recall unease, suspicion, and earlier sightings they had at the time.
The broken promise, he did let him in but he did not keep his promise, demonstrates that an attacker's words are instruments, not contracts.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests intuition as pre-incident-indicator processing: the unease Kelly felt at the stranger's voice arrived before she could name a reason, and de Becker argues such feelings are logical computations running below conscious awareness. The book's evidence is case-based: Kelly's first signal was genuine data, and the politeness-guilt override that made her suppress it is the same denial dynamic the chapter names as the enemy of successful prediction.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Vocal tone and offer-of-help behavior at first contact
assets.question: Kelly did not like that voice; right from the start something just sounded wrong. What was the cue her intuition had actually registered?
assets.correct_cue: A stranger called out that he would bring the can up and volunteered to carry her groceries before she asked for anything. The genuine cue is the pairing of an uninvited offer with persistence that overrides her refusals: he disqualifies her twice, saying she does not look like she has got it, and then tugs at a bag she is still holding. Kelly's instant, inexplicable aversion to the voice was her intuition processing these pre-incident indicators, the spontaneous bid for contact and the refusal to accept no, before her conscious mind could name them. de Becker's point is that this early feeling was real data, not rudeness or paranoia, and that politeness and guilt are exactly the forces that talk people out of acting on it.
distractors: The torn grocery bag and the cans of cat food rolling down the stairs, a packaging accident unrelated to the man's intent.
His friendly smile and courteous manner, which are precisely the tools predators use to mask intent, so a smile is not evidence of safety.
The fact that he said he was late because of a broken watch, a detail offered to explain hurry rather than a signal of danger in itself.
assets.underlying_psychology: The scenario tests pre-incident indicators processed by intuition: detectable factors, the unprovoked offer of help and persistence against refusal, occurred before the assault outcome, and Kelly registered them below conscious awareness. de Becker argues intuition is a logical process that runs faster than conscious reasoning, and that the guilt people feel for suspecting a friendly stranger is a social override that suppresses the very signal that would protect them.

assets.topic: The Closed Window (Incongruous Action as Survival Signal)
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen shows the bedroom of Kelly's apartment after the assault. The young man, now fully dressed, stands by the window: he closes it, glances at his watch, and begins moving with exaggerated haste while speaking to Kelly, who is still on the bed. A timestamp scrubber and a behavior-mismatch counter let the player compare each action against his announced story.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the footage and identify the one action that contradicts the man's stated plan to leave. Then explain what that contradiction reveals about his true intent.
key_concepts: The man was already dressed and had announced he was leaving when he closed Kelly's window, an action with no place in his stated plan.
Kelly's own realization: noise was the thing, that is why he closed the window, and that is how she knew.
He had to be concerned about noise because he planned to use the gun inside the apartment, where neighbors could hear it.
The unprompted promise, I promise I'm not going to hurt you, was a manufactured reassurance that comes out of nowhere only when there is a reason for it.
His hurry was staged: dressing, watch-checking, and claiming he had to be somewhere compose a performance of departure, not a departure.
Kelly heard drawers being opened in the kitchen while he claimed to be getting a drink, the sound of a man searching for a knife.
The text's conclusion is that he wanted a knife because using the gun would be too noisy.
Incongruity between behavior and stated story is a survival signal: the closed window meant the opposite of leaving.
It was genuine fear, not like when we are startled, that gave Kelly the courage to act without hesitation.
The fear told her to be quiet and not doubt it, and she described herself as a passenger moving down that hallway.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the survival-signal mechanism of incongruity: a dressed man about to leave has no reason to close a window, so the gesture was evidence of a planned gunshot and a concern about noise. de Becker builds the claim from Kelly's case, noise was the thing, that is why he closed the window, and pairs it with the unsolicited promise to show how actions, not words, carry the signal.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Incongruous action during a staged exit
assets.question: Why did the closed window tell Kelly her attacker planned to kill her?
assets.correct_cue: The man announced he was leaving, was already dressed, and had no reason to touch the window, yet he closed it. The cue is the incongruity: a man preparing to walk out a door does not seal a window against noise unless he expects a loud event inside the room. Kelly finally articulated it herself: noise was the thing, that is why he closed the window. Combined with the unprompted promise that he would not hurt her and his trip to the kitchen, where Kelly heard drawers being opened, the actions pointed to one plan: he wanted a knife because using the gun would be too noisy, and he intended to use it on her.
distractors: He closed the window because the room felt chilly, a comfort motive the text never suggests for a man supposedly rushing out.
He was closing it to keep her cat inside, a fiction the text does not support; his own story was about a hungry cat, not an escaped one.
He was securing the apartment before leaving, since protecting someone else's property is not a behavior of an attacker mid-assault.
assets.underlying_psychology: The scenario tests the survival-signal mechanism of incongruity: when actions contradict a stated story, intuition detects the mismatch even when conscious reasoning cannot. de Becker argues this kind of fear is a rational response to detectable pre-incident indicators, the noise-sealing gesture and the invented promise, and that naming the contradiction is what converts dread into a usable prediction.

assets.topic: The Quarter-Inch Thumb (Micro-Movements Over Gross Movement)
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen shows a living room frozen in time: a woman in black slacks and a man's white shirt holds a small semi-automatic pistol on her husband, who stands with his hands outstretched. An overturned table, a phone off the hook, and a broken glass litter the floor. A magnification lens lets the player zoom in on the woman's right hand as she nervously changes her grip.
assets.player_mission: Zoom into the scene and select the small detail that carries the most predictive weight. Then judge which of the cluttered details are snapshots without meaning and which is the portrait that completes the prediction.
key_concepts: The quarter-inch movement of the woman's thumb onto the pistol's hammer was the scene's most significant detail.
de Becker states the fraction of an inch the thumb traveled to rest on the hammer carried the woman further along the path to homicide than anything she had said or could have said.
Gross movements may get our attention, but they are rarely the ones that matter most.
Pulling the hammer back was a not-so-subtle underscoring that earned her new credibility.
Details are snapshots, not portraits; the bare feet, overturned table, phone off the hook, and broken glass were assessed and discarded.
Pre-incident indicators are those detectable factors that occur before the outcome being predicted.
Everything a person does is created twice, once in the mind and once in its execution, so ideas and impulses are pre-incident indicators for action.
Stepping on the first rung of a ladder is a pre-incident indicator to reaching the top; stepping on the sixth even more so.
The woman's threats revealed the idea, and introducing the gun into the argument, plus its purchase some months earlier, were earlier rungs on the same ladder.
The best predictions use all the time available and complete just behind the line between foresight and hindsight.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests pre-incident indicators in high-stakes prediction: the quarter-inch movement of a thumb to a pistol's hammer outranked everything said in the room. de Becker claims small motor details index intent better than gross movements, and that the best predictions use all available time, completing just behind the line between foresight and hindsight.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Micro-movement of the hand on a weapon
assets.question: With the pistol pointed at her husband, which detail moved the woman furthest along the path to homicide?
assets.correct_cue: While the woman was nervously changing her grip on the pistol, her thumb traveled just a quarter of an inch to rest on the hammer of the gun. de Becker read this micro-movement as the detail of great significance: the fraction of an inch her thumb traveled to rest on the hammer carried the woman further along the path to homicide than anything she had said or could have said. Seconds later she pulled the hammer back, a not-so-subtle underscoring that earned her new credibility. The gross elements of the scene, the overturned table, the phone off the hook, the broken glass, and her bare feet, were assessed and quickly discarded as snapshots rather than portraits.
distractors: Her missing shoes, a detail de Becker explicitly noticed and discarded as irrelevant to his task.
The phone knocked off the hook, debris from the argument that he assessed and discarded.
The rapid shallow breaths of the husband, his own fear response rather than evidence of her intent.
assets.underlying_psychology: The scenario tests pre-incident-indicator analysis in high-stakes prediction: the book's rule is that gross movements get our attention but are rarely the ones that matter most, while small motor actions such as the thumb-to-hammer movement index intent more reliably. de Becker claims the best predictions use all the time available and complete themselves just behind the line that separates foresight and hindsight.

assets.topic: The Retreat That Wasn't (Backing Away as Final Indicator)
assets.visual_frame_description: The living-room tableau continues: the woman with the pistol begins stepping backward away from her husband, increasing the distance between them while keeping the weapon trained on him. The screen shows a distance meter and a prediction-completion meter filling toward the trigger moment.
assets.player_mission: Decide what the backward movement means and whether it completes the prediction. Then choose the correct reading of spatial withdrawal during an armed confrontation.
key_concepts: Backing away from her husband looked like retreat but was the final pre-incident indicator before the pulling of the trigger.
Guns are not intimate weapons, so the shooting of a gun calls for distance between shooter and target.
The woman's desire for some distance from the person she was about to shoot was the element that completed the prediction.
The boy acted the instant he registered the withdrawal, and the gunshot sounded a moment later; he was startled, but not surprised.
The pistol had stayed steadily pointed at her husband throughout the scene, including during the retreat.
The silence that followed the first shot concerned him more than the noise itself, because he could not hear what was happening.
The forces that inhibit violence and those that might provoke it were rising and falling against each other like stormy waves.
The book distinguishes genuine danger-based fear from startle, movie fear, and the fear of public speaking.
After discharging the shots, the woman shifted to the role of supportive wife nursing her husband's injury, as if she had played no part in it.
de Becker's childhood reading of this scene later became the basis of MOSAIC, the automated threat-assessment system he designed.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests weapon-specific posture reading: because guns are not intimate weapons, the woman's backward step was approach-to-action rather than retreat. de Becker's evidence is the prediction he made and acted on a moment before the gunshot, startled but not surprised, demonstrating that spatial withdrawal can be the final pre-incident indicator.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Why did the woman backing away from her husband signal that she was about to shoot, the opposite of de-escalation?
assets.correct_cue: To a casual observer the retreat looked like backing off, but the observer read it as the final pre-incident indicator before the pulling of the trigger. The reasoning: guns are not intimate weapons, and a person about to fire wants distance from the target, not closeness. Her desire for some distance from the person she was about to shoot was the element that completed the prediction, and he moved the instant he registered it; the gunshot followed a moment later.
distractors: The withdrawal meant she was calming down and would put the gun down, which misreads distance-seeking as de-escalation.
She was retreating to gain a better position to negotiate, though the text describes no negotiating behavior, only silence and withdrawal.
She was giving her husband space to escape, though her weapon remained steadily pointed during the retreat.
assets.underlying_psychology: The scenario tests the mechanism of weapon-specific posture reading: because a gun is not an intimate weapon, increasing distance is approach-to-action behavior rather than a retreat from conflict. de Becker presents the incident as automatic pre-incident-indicator processing learned under high stakes, showing that final indicators can be spatial rather than verbal.

assets.topic: Words That Betray (Threats and the Advance-or-Retreat Rule)
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen replays the armed confrontation: the woman repeats that she is going to kill her husband, quietly, almost to herself, then falls silent, then alternates between an angry tirade and muted pauses. A word-bubble layer annotates each threat with its function, showing the threats as communications rather than mere noise.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the threats and assess what the words reveal about the speaker's position. Then pick the correct reading of what a threat admits and which choice it forces on the speaker.
key_concepts: Threats are easy to speak and harder to honor.
A threat betrays the speaker by admitting her failure to influence events in any other way.
Everyone who threatens must advance or retreat; the threat forces a binary decision.
The woman might have been satisfied with the fear her words and actions caused and left it at that.
Or she might pull the trigger, and the text warns that violence is the last thing some people do.
Her quiet pauses were ambiguous: they could be a rallying of reason or a contemplation of murder.
The threatener's hostility and silence alternated as the forces inhibiting and provoking violence rose and fell like stormy waves.
The chapter claims that even the violence we call random and senseless is neither; it always has purpose and meaning to the perpetrator.
de Becker's rule for exploring suspects: no theory is too remote to explore, no person is beyond consideration, no gut feeling is too unsubstantiated.

When asked who could have sent the threats rather than who they think sent them, victims freely list every person with the ability, then assign motives, and in almost every case one imaginative theory is correct.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests threat analysis: threats are communications that admit the speaker's failure to influence events any other way and force an advance-or-retreat decision. de Becker's case evidence is the woman with the gun, whose quiet pauses could not tell whether they were a rallying of reason or a contemplation of murder, so prediction had to rest on pre-incident indicators rather than on words.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: The content and timing of spoken threats
assets.question: What did the woman's threats reveal about her position, and what did they force her to do?
assets.correct_cue: The threats betrayed her by admitting her failure to influence events in any other way, and like all people who threaten, she had to advance or retreat. The cue is the admission embedded in the threat itself: to threaten is to confess that persuasion, negotiation, and all other influence channels have failed, leaving only the option to follow through or back down. Her alternating hostility and silence meant the forces inhibiting violence and provoking it were rising and falling against each other, and her quiet pauses had to be assessed as a rallying of reason or a contemplation of murder.
distractors: The threat proved she was only bluffing, since threats are easy to speak, but some threateners do advance, as this one did.
Her silence was a reliable sign she was calming down, yet silence can equally be a contemplation of murder.
The threat was meaningless because a gun makes an outcome certain, though the threat's meaning is communicative, not physical.
assets.underlying_psychology: The scenario tests the mechanism of threat analysis: threats are communications that admit the speaker's failure of influence and force an advance-or-retreat decision. de Becker warns that quiet pauses after threats are ambiguous, a rallying of reason or a contemplation of murder, so the prediction must be built from pre-incident indicators rather than from the words alone.

assets.topic: Case 6284-C: The Promise That Came Out of Nowhere
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen presents a digital evidence folder labeled Case 6284-C. The left panel holds a timestamped timeline of the attacker's actions inside Kelly's apartment, the center shows freeze frames of the bedroom and kitchen, and the bottom holds a transcript of the attacker's lines. The player works through the file like an investigator preparing a prediction brief.
assets.player_mission: Audit the case file: compare the attacker's stated plan against the timed behavior log, then issue the correct diagnosis of his intent and rank the three competing verdicts.
key_concepts: The attacker's promise served compliance, not truth: its purpose was to keep Kelly still.
A closed window while dressed and supposedly leaving pointed to noise control for a planned gunshot.
Kelly heard drawers being opened in the kitchen during the claimed trip to get a drink.
The text's conclusion is that he was looking for a knife because using the gun would be too noisy.
He was not Kelly's first victim; he had killed one of his other victims, stabbing her to death.
Kelly's profound fear arrived only when she knew he planned to kill her, and the fear was informative rather than disabling.
A promise that comes out of nowhere is itself a survival signal in the book's framework.
Kelly's earlier failure to follow signals, including finally handing over the grocery bag, had put her at risk in the first place.
Listening to one small survival signal saved her life.
After acting on the signal, Kelly felt new confidence in herself and was tired of being blamed and blaming herself.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests deception detection through behavioral congruence: the attacker's stated plan to leave was contradicted by his actions, the closed window, the watch check, and the opened drawers. de Becker's theory is that survival signals are best concealed when an attacker is not known to us but still leak through incongruous behavior, and the assessment is observational, based on Kelly's case rather than controlled research.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Did the attacker intend to release Kelly after the assault, or did his post-assault behavior reveal an intent to kill her?
assets.subject_baseline: A friendly-looking young man, cordial and gentlemanly, who had earlier introduced himself to Kelly by volunteering to carry her groceries on the apartment stairs. Kelly did not know his history, but the text confirms he was not her first victim and that he had killed one of his other victims by stabbing her to death.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 0:00 He gets up from the bed, fully dressed. 0:12 He closes the window. 0:20 He glances at his watch. 0:30 He begins acting as if he is in a hurry. 0:45 He waves the gun and issues instructions for her to stay where she is. 1:10 He walks to the kitchen saying he wants a drink. 1:40 Drawers are heard being opened in the kitchen.
assets.interrogation_transcript: He says: I gotta be somewhere. Hey, don't look so scared. I promise I'm not going to hurt you. He adds: I'm going to the kitchen to get something to drink, and then I'll leave. I promise. But you stay right where you are. Kelly assures him: You know I won't move. The instant he steps from the room, Kelly stands up and follows him, pulling the sheet off the bed with her, and walks out her front door while he is in the kitchen.
assets.correct_diagnosis: He planned to kill Kelly. The promise was manufactured for compliance, and the behavioral sequence, dressing, sealing the window, checking the time, hurrying, and searching the kitchen drawers, is the behavior of a man staging an exit in order to kill her silently.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The window is the decisive evidence: he was dressed and supposedly leaving, so he had no reason to close it except to control the noise of a gunshot. His promise contradicted his hurry and came out of nowhere, and unsolicited reassurances are a survival signal. The kitchen drawers were unnecessary for getting a drink; Kelly heard him opening them because he was looking for a knife, since using the gun would be too noisy. Every element of the log contradicts his stated plan to walk out the door.
distractors: He genuinely intended to leave, since the hurry, the watch checks, and the line about having to be somewhere support a real departure.
He closed the window as a courtesy to secure the apartment before leaving.
He went to the kitchen for a drink exactly as he said, and the drawer sounds were incidental house noise.

assets.topic: Case 6291-B: The Woman Who Promised to Kill
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen presents Case 6291-B as a forensic dossier: a police-style timeline of the living-room confrontation with still frames of the thumb-on-hammer moment, the hammer being cocked, and the backward step. An evidence list logs the gun's purchase months earlier, the threats, and the position of the two children in the house.
assets.player_mission: Review the timed log and issue a murder-prediction verdict before the final frame. Then justify the verdict with the pre-incident indicators in order of importance.
key_concepts: The purchase of the pistol months earlier was an early rung in a ladder of pre-incident indicators.
Introducing the gun into the argument was another rung, and the threats revealed the idea.
The thumb-on-hammer micro-movement outweighed everything the woman said.
Cocking the hammer was a not-so-subtle underscoring that earned her new credibility.
Backing away sealed the prediction because guns are not intimate weapons.
The best predictions use all the time available and complete just behind the line between foresight and hindsight.
When the shot finally came, the boy was startled, but not surprised.
The silence after the shot concerned him more than the gunfire itself, until the following shots came.
Afterward she shifted to the role of supportive wife, nursing her husband's injury as if she had played no part in it.
The childhood analysis of this scene became the basis for MOSAIC, which screens threats to justices of the U.S. Supreme Court.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests cumulative pre-incident indicators: threats, the gun purchase, thumb-to-hammer contact, cocking, and distance-seeking each added a rung toward the predicted shot. de Becker presents the analysis as the origin of his prediction method, later systematized in the MOSAIC assessment system; the basis is observational case experience rather than controlled studies.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Would the woman pointing a small semi-automatic pistol at her husband fire the gun, or would she settle for the fear and attention she had already created?
assets.subject_baseline: A thirty-three-year-old woman, attractive and slender, wearing black slacks and a man's white shirt, a mother of two who earlier that year lived in a house with an argumentative marriage and two small children. Months before the confrontation she had bought the small pistol that was now in her hand, and the gun held eight bullets.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: Start The pistol is pointed steadily at her husband, who barely moves, his hands held out stiffly in front of him; she changes her grip anxiously. 1:00 She is by turns hostile, then silent; the pistol never wavers. 2:30 A quarter-inch movement: her thumb comes to rest on the hammer of the gun. 3:00 An angry tirade begins, her words chopped and spit across the room. 3:20 She pulls the hammer of the pistol back. 4:10 She begins backing away from her husband, increasing distance. 4:20 The gunshot. 4:30 Silence. 4:45 Several more gunshots fired quickly.
assets.interrogation_transcript: She repeats quietly, almost to herself: Now I'm going to kill you. The observer notes there are eight bullets in the gun and that the stakes include two young children in the house, including a toddler napping in a bedroom. After the shots, she leans over her wounded husband, seemingly offering care, telling the family she will deal with the police and the ambulance.
assets.correct_diagnosis: She fired the gun. The pre-incident indicators, buying the gun months earlier, introducing it into the argument, thumb-to-hammer contact, cocking the hammer, and finally backing away for distance, cumulatively predicted the shot, which the observer announced a moment before it sounded.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Each element is a pre-incident indicator occurring before the outcome: ideas and impulses precede actions, so the threats revealed the idea and the gun's purchase months earlier was another rung on the same ladder. The thumb on the hammer carried her further toward homicide than anything she said; cocking the hammer added credibility; and because guns are not intimate weapons, her withdrawal signaled the final step before pulling the trigger. The prediction completed just behind the line between foresight and hindsight, and the shot came a moment later.
distractors: She would be satisfied with the fear her words and actions caused and leave it at that, a retreat the observer explicitly weighed and rejected because the indicators kept advancing.
Her husband would disarm her during her pauses, though he barely moved, frozen in the gun sights with his hands outstretched.
She would fire past him to frighten him, though the pistol stayed trained on him and the final distance-seeking indicated an aimed shot.

assets.topic: Case 6212-A: The Suspect She Hated to Name
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen presents Case 6212-A: a meeting room where a couple reviews a suspect board with their consultant. The wife narrates each candidate while a heat-map behind her highlights her body language: the hesitation, the lowered gaze, and the apologetic pause before she names the person she has no concrete reasons to suspect.
assets.player_mission: Track which candidate is named with reasons versus which one surfaces as an uneasy feeling, and issue the correct diagnosis of the caller's identity.
key_concepts: Victims of anonymous threats know more than they think they know; the information is trapped inside them where the consultant can help find it.
Asking who could have sent the threats rather than who they think sent them frees victims to list everyone with the ability.
Assigning a motive, even a ridiculous one, to each person on the list is a creative process that puts them under no pressure to be correct.
In almost every case, one of the client's imaginative theories will be correct.
The person the client names with no concrete reasons and an uneasy feeling is almost always the caller.
de Becker describes his main job as getting the pieces of the puzzle onto the table.
He refuses to call the problem a mystery, calling it instead a puzzle in which there are enough pieces available to reveal what the image is.
Every puzzle can be solved long before all the pieces are in place.
No theory is too remote to explore, no person is beyond consideration, and no gut feeling is too unsubstantiated.
In the book's claim, every intuition is firmly substantiated.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests intuition as recovered local expertise: the victim holds the information about her own case, and freeing her from the pressure to be correct lets it surface. de Becker's method, asking who could have sent the threats and then assigning motives, is designed to bypass the denial that protects people from suspecting those they know, and he reports that the intuition-named suspect is almost always the caller.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Which person was making the harassing and threatening phone calls to the couple?
assets.subject_baseline: A married couple who came to the consultant to identify the caller. Their relationship was stable and their reporting lucid; both were confident the caller was someone they knew because of what the caller said. The wife invariably produced the decisive information during the discussion of suspects.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: During the suspect review the wife names obvious candidates: her ex-husband, the man who used to rent a room from them, a neighbor angry about their construction work, and the contractor they fired. Then she pauses, drops her gaze, hesitates, and volunteers that there is one other person she has no concrete reason to suspect; she just has this feeling, and she hates to even suggest it.
assets.interrogation_transcript: The wife says: You know, there is one other person, and I don't have any concrete reasons for thinking it's him. I just have this feeling, and I hate to even suggest it, but. The consultant comments: right there I could send them home and send my bill, because that is who it will be. He tells every client: no theory is too remote to explore, no person is beyond consideration, no gut feeling is too unsubstantiated.
assets.correct_diagnosis: The caller was the person the wife named on intuition, the suspect she had no concrete reasons for naming and hated to suggest. The consultant's rule is that the intuition-named suspect is the caller, and his contribution is to give clients permission to listen to themselves.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The couple had the experience of their own case; the consultant's contribution was to get the pieces on the table. He never asks who they think sent the threats, a question victims cannot answer because they cannot imagine anyone they know did it, but who could have sent them, which frees people to list everyone with the ability and then assign a motive, even a ridiculous one, to each person. In almost every case one imaginative theory is correct, and most often it is the one that surfaced as an uneasy feeling the client was embarrassed to voice.
distractors: The ex-husband, because his motive was obvious, though he was named with reasons, precisely the category intuition did not flag.
The fired contractor, because he had a grievance, a logical suspect with concrete reasons rather than the intuition-driven pick.
The neighbor angry about the construction work, visible friction, but named with reasons rather than feeling.

assets.topic: Case 6230-D: The Murder the News Called Unpredictable
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen presents a television news story as an evidence exhibit: the report plays while cards list each fact the reporter states, the threats, the firing from his job, the gun put to the wife's head a week earlier, the stalking, and the same-day restraining order, followed by the closing claim that no one could have predicted it.
assets.player_mission: Audit the broadcast against the pre-incident-indicator framework and render a verdict on whether the homicide was predictable from the facts the report itself supplied.
key_concepts: The news story itself reported threats, a job firing, a gun put to the wife's head a week before the killing, and stalking.
A restraining order had been served on the man the same day as his divorce papers, coincidentally also his birthday.
The reporter still concluded that officials concede no one could have predicted this would happen.
de Becker says we want to believe people are infinitely complex because then we have no duty to anticipate violence.
As long as violence remains a mystery, we need feel no responsibility for failing to read signals.
In service of these comfortable myths, victims suffer and criminals prosper.
The human violence we call random and senseless is neither; it always has purpose and meaning to the perpetrator.
By finding the perpetrator's humanness, his similarity to us, such an act can be predicted.
Homicide is now the leading cause of death for women in the workplace.
Only 20 percent of all homicides are committed by strangers; the other 80 percent are committed by people we know.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests denial as the enemy of prediction: every reported fact, threats, stalking, a prior gun-to-head, and same-day divorce papers, pointed toward violence, yet officials declared it unpredictable. de Becker argues that labeling violence senseless relieves us of the duty to anticipate it, and in service of these comfortable myths, victims suffer and criminals prosper.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Was the killing of the woman at her workplace predictable from the facts the news story itself reported?
assets.subject_baseline: A man whose marriage was ending: he had been threatening his wife for some time, had been fired from his job, had stalked her, and a week before the killing had put a gun to her head. A restraining order was served on him the same day as his divorce papers, which was also his birthday.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: The news report numbers the behaviors in sequence: threats; termination from his job; a gun put to his wife's head the week before; stalking of her; the restraining order and divorce papers delivered the same day; then the shooting of his wife at her work.
assets.interrogation_transcript: The reporter's closing line: officials concede that no-one could have predicted this would happen. The chapter notes the story had just reported the man's threats, his being fired from his job, his putting a gun to his wife's head the week before the killing, and his stalking of her.
assets.correct_diagnosis: The homicide was eminently predictable; the officials' claim is the culture's denial talking, not an honest limit of prediction. Every major element the book gives for forecasting violence, threats, recent job loss, stalking, a prior gun-to-head, and the same-day divorce papers, is present in the report itself.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Threats are pre-incident indicators because ideas precede impulses and impulses precede actions; stalking is the textbook pursuit behavior de Becker predicts daily; a gun put to the victim's head a week earlier is a prior rung of the same ladder; and the divorce papers delivered that day remove restraints while the birthday frames the day as significant to him. The book's claim is that we want to believe violence is beyond understanding because as long as it remains a mystery we have no duty to anticipate it, and in service of these comfortable myths, victims suffer and criminals prosper.
distractors: The killing was a sudden psychotic break with no warning, which is contradicted by the reported threats, stalking, and the prior gun incident.
Restraining orders and divorce paperwork reliably de-escalate such situations, though the book treats them as factors in an unfolding sequence rather than guarantees.
Spousal killings at work are too rare to foresee, though the text reports homicide is the leading cause of death for women in the workplace.

assets.topic: Case 6299-E: The Victims Who Said Out of Nowhere
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen presents a debrief room: a survivor sits across from an interviewer. The first frame plays the instant answer, that it just came out of nowhere, then the room falls into silence and the player watches the amended account surface: unease at first meeting, suspicion when approached, a car seen earlier that day.
assets.player_mission: Time-code both statements, compare what was said before the pause with what came after it, and issue a diagnosis of what actually happened at the moment of the encounter.
key_concepts: Asked whether they could have seen the violence coming, most victims answer: no, it just came out of nowhere.
If the interviewer is quiet and waits a moment, the information arrives: I felt uneasy when I first met that guy.
The follow-up statements include being suspicious when he approached and realizing the car had been seen earlier in the day.
If they realize it now, they knew it then, in the book's claim.
There is a universal code of violence, and most of it is in you.
Denial is the powerful and cunning enemy of successful predictions.
The belief that one could be a victim at some time is a key element in recognizing when you are in the presence of danger.
Denial is a save-now-pay-later scheme whose fall is far greater when victimization actually occurs.
Denial causes a constant low-grade anxiety and keeps people from taking action that could reduce the risks.
People compartmentalize hazards to exclude themselves: that is in the inner city, I am not in a relationship now, or you are only at risk if you are out late at night.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests hindsight and denial in post-violence self-report: victims say it came out of nowhere and, moments later, recall the unease, suspicion, and earlier car sightings they had at the time. de Becker's claim is that if they realize it now, they knew it then, a universal code of violence available to everyone, which he supports with case interviews rather than controlled data.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: After violence, when victims say it came out of nowhere, did they actually have no warning, or did they have signals they did not follow?
assets.subject_baseline: Clients debriefed after suffering violence, survivors of assaults, attacks, and intrusions across the consultant's years of casework. Their immediate answer is uniform: that it just came out of nowhere.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: Their answer is instantaneous, then the interviewer goes quiet and waits. After the pause the same people amend the record: they felt uneasy when they first met that guy, they were suspicious when he approached them, or they realize now they had seen that car earlier in the day.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Question: could you have seen this coming? Answer: no, it just came out of nowhere. A beat of silence. Then: I felt uneasy when I first met that guy. Or: now that I think of it, I was suspicious when he approached me. Or: I realize now I had seen that car earlier in the day. The consultant's comment: of course, if they realize it now, they knew it then. We all see the signals because there is a universal code of violence.
assets.correct_diagnosis: The victims did have warning signals at the time, unease, suspicion, a familiar car seen earlier, and they suppressed them for the same reason everyone suppresses them: to preserve the comfortable belief that violence happens without warning to others. The diagnosis is denial operating at the moment of the encounter, not unpredictability.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The out-of-nowhere claim and the remembered unease are the same memory examined twice: the information was present before the outcome, which is the definition of a pre-incident indicator. Denial, the chapter's named enemy of successful predictions, keeps people from acting on the feeling that their intuition had already registered, the unease at first meeting. The consultant's conclusion is that everyone sees the signals because there is a universal code of violence, and most of it is in you.
distractors: Victims genuinely received no signals, which is contradicted by their own recalled unease and suspicion when prompted.
The memories are confabulated after the fact, though the book treats them as recovered information the person knew then.
Signal detection requires expert training victims lack, though the book's thesis is that every person already has the gift and mainly needs permission to use it.

assets.topic: Boss Battle: Kelly's Walk Out of the Apartment
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen shows a battle arena rendered as a chessboard corridor: Kelly's apartment, the hallway, and the neighbors' door across the landing. The attacker's actions, the window closing, the watch glance, and the promise bubble, appear as glowing tokens that the player must assemble into a staged-exit pattern before the kitchen door opens.
assets.player_mission: Read the staged-exit tokens, then choose the escape move that resolves the battle, timing the exit to the instant his back is turned at the kitchen. The battle is won when you and the neighbors are behind a locked door.
key_concepts: The closed window, the watch check, and the announced hurry contradicted the story of a simple departure.
The unsolicited promise that he would not hurt her was a manufactured reassurance: Kelly knew he was lying.
The genuine fear Kelly felt was the powerful ally that says to do what it tells you to do.
It was the first time since the incident began that she felt profound fear.
She described herself as a passenger moving down that hallway, action without deliberation.
She walked out her front door leaving it ajar, crossed the hall, and locked the neighbors' door behind her, signaling them to be quiet.
She somehow knew the apartment across the hall would be unlocked.
She knew that if she had stayed in the room, he would come back from the kitchen and kill her.
The drawers in the kitchen meant he was searching for a knife, since using the gun would be too noisy.
Kelly's earlier failure to follow signals, including finally letting go of the grocery bag, had put her at risk in the first place.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the survival-signal-to-action mechanism: the staged exit, the window, the watch, and the promise, is read as preparation to kill, and genuine fear converts prediction into movement. de Becker's claim is that real fear, not startle or worry, is a rational ally that directs behavior, as with Kelly walking out while the man searched the kitchen drawers.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests the chapter's core claim that real fear is a reliable ally and that survival signals, actions contradicting a stated story, unlock escape. Kelly's escape worked because she read the attacker's staged-exit sequence, dressed, window closed, watch checked, promise offered, and then acted on the fear it generated, moving while he believed she was still immobilized by compliance.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are Kelly, lying still on the bed in your apartment. The man who assaulted you is now dressed and on his feet. He closes the window, glances at his watch, and announces he is in a hurry, saying he has to be somewhere. He adds: don't look so scared, I promise I'm not going to hurt you. The scene freezes and you must identify what the sequence means.
assets.stage_1_question: Given that he says he is leaving, what does the combination of his actions tell you about his actual plan?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: His plan is not to leave; it is to kill you before he leaves. The closed window proves he is planning for noise control, a gunshot, the watch check and the hurry are stage business for a man who intends to act, and the unsolicited promise is the confession that he has a reason to reassure you: he needs you compliant. A promise not to hurt you issued out of nowhere is the opposite of reassurance.
assets.stage_2_intervention: He waves the gun and says not to move or do anything; he is going to the kitchen to get something to drink and then he will leave, promising, but tells you to stay right where you are. The instant he steps out of the room you hear drawers being opened in the kitchen. You cannot see him. You are alone with the sound of drawers. Make your move now.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Leave immediately and silently: stand up, stay close behind him so his back is turned, slip out your front door leaving it ajar, cross the hall to the neighbors' apartment, lock their door behind you, and hold a finger up to signal them to be quiet. Do not obey the stay-put instruction, which exists to keep you available, and do not wait for the drink. The drawers are the sound of him looking for a knife to do the job quietly, and the reason he closed the window was so the neighbors would not hear the shot.

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Ten-Year-Old in the Hallway
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen shows the living room as a prediction maze: household debris rendered as low-priority tiles and the woman's right hand as a glowing focal point. A foresight meter fills as the player identifies each pre-incident indicator, and the maze resolves into the hallway leading to the child's bedroom.
assets.player_mission: Identify the decisive detail in the room, read the final spatial indicator, and move your piece out of the room before the shot fires. Win the battle by completing the prediction just behind the line between foresight and hindsight.
key_concepts: Pre-incident indicators are those detectable factors that occur before the outcome being predicted.
Stepping on the first rung of a ladder is a pre-incident indicator to reaching the top; stepping on the sixth even more so.
Everything a person does is created twice, once in the mind and once in its execution.
Ideas and impulses are pre-incident indicators for action.
The mother's threats revealed the idea, and the gun's purchase some months earlier was an earlier indicator.
The thumb on the hammer carried her further along the path to homicide than anything she said.
Cocking the hammer was a not-so-subtle underscoring that earned her new credibility.
Because guns are not intimate weapons, backing away was the final pre-incident indicator before the trigger.
The best predictions use all the time available and complete just behind the line between foresight and hindsight.
When the gunshot came, the boy was startled, but not surprised.
That childhood reading of pre-incident indicators became the model for MOSAIC, the assessment system used to screen threats to justices of the U.S. Supreme Court.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests pre-incident-indicator processing under time pressure: the thumb-to-hammer micro-movement and the final distance-seeking withdrawal complete a prediction of the shot. de Becker's evidence is autobiographical, the ten-year-old's reading of the scene preceded the gunshot by a moment, and he states it later became the logic of the MOSAIC threat-assessment system.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests pre-incident indicators, which the book calls the single most important tool of any prediction: detectable factors that occur before the outcome being predicted. The player must separate snapshot details from portrait details, use all the time available, and act when the final indicator appears, completing the prediction just behind the line between foresight and hindsight.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are ten years old, standing off to the side in a doorway, watching your mother hold a small semi-automatic pistol on your stepfather, whose hands are stretched out stiffly in front of him. Two young children, including a toddler napping in a bedroom, are in the house. The floor holds an overturned table, a phone knocked off the hook, and a broken glass. Your mother is barefoot. The gun has eight bullets and is pointed steadily at him. She repeats quietly: now I'm going to kill you.
assets.stage_1_question: One detail in this room matters more than all the others combined. Which one, and why?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Her thumb traveling a quarter of an inch to rest on the hammer of the gun. The gross scene, the chaos, the broken glass, and her bare feet, draws the eye, but the gross movements may get our attention even though they are rarely the ones that matter most. The thumb-on-hammer is a micro-movement of intent that carries her further along the path to homicide than anything she has said; a moment later she cocks the hammer, a not-so-subtle underscoring that earned her new credibility.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Freed from her tirade, the woman begins backing away from her husband, gaining distance while the gun stays trained on him. The room's silence deepens. You have time, because the best predictions use all the time available, but the sequence is completing. What does her retreat mean, and what do you do in the next instant?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The backing away is not retreat or de-escalation; it is the final pre-incident indicator before the trigger, because guns are not intimate weapons and a shooter wants distance from the target. Act at once: back quietly down the hall, through the kitchen past the burning and forgotten dinner, into the small bedroom where the young girl is napping, and move the child out of the line of fire. The gunshot sounds a moment later; you are startled, but not surprised, and the silence that follows concerns you more than the shot itself.
